title: Gateless Barrier, Case 24: Feng-hsueh: Equality and Differentiation
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The teacher's talk emphasizes the importance of embracing the present moment, letting go of notions of before and after, and finding balance between silence and speech. This involves acknowledging both the beauty and imperfection of each, rather than trying to transcend or escape one or the other. By doing so, we can cultivate mindfulness and presence, find our place in life without conceptual thinking, and approach our practice with humility and openness, ultimately showing up for our life as it is, with all its suffering and joy.
topics: Dogen's teachings on finding one's place where they are

sentences.text: Good morning, everybody.
Good morning.
I wasn't terribly late, but I was down to the wire getting ready, and I had a memory.
One time, some time ago, in the previous dharma hall, at the top of the Masonic Lodge, which had a bright red floor.
That was its main character.
Norman was here for a weekend retreat or something, and Bob must have been there.
We were waiting for the talk to start, and he didn't show up.
We were waiting and waiting, and remember this?
We were standing there, trying to be so good, waiting and waiting and waiting.
Five minutes, ten minutes, I don't know how long it was.
This isn't a very good story, because I don't remember the punch line, I just remember the waiting.
Eventually somebody went down there.
I think we had access to a room downstairs, which was like his meeting room, or prep room, or something.
So I think maybe he was just mixed up about the time.
I can't remember, but I remember the waiting.
That made me think of an earlier time, one of the first times, sometime in the early 90s.
Florence Caplow, who, along with Bob and me, was one of the founders, had this great idea to have a lecture series.
Pretty early on.
I don't know how we thought we could do this.
We invited this guy named Steve, I forget his last name, but he had been abbot at Hartford Street Zen Center in San Francisco.
He took over from Issan Dorsey, which was like a pop-up Zen hospice.

He had taken over not just the Zen Center and the hospice from Issan Dorsey, but also all the problems and challenges that happened when Issan, one day, pretty much, as far as I understand it, just brought some of his friends with AIDS home.
Didn't get any licenses or permits, no board meetings or anything like that.
Which is a great tradition in Zen.
You're supposed to just do stuff, consequences be damned.
I'm not very good at that.
Anyway, Steve, I'll think of his last name in a minute, happened to be up in the area.
He was on sabbatical on Orcas Island.
Florence knew about that and invited him.
He was an important person in the American Zen world, and he was going to come give a talk to this tiny little brand new sitting group in Bellingham.
He misunderstood how the ferries worked or something, so he wasn't just five or ten minutes late.
He was two and a half hours late.
And same thing: we're just going to wait.
But you know who were the best waiters of all?
The teachers of our Shambhala Center, Paul and Jenny Warwick, who had been students of Choyon Trampa, early students of Trampa Rinpoche.
They were really impressive.
They just sat down in meditation and didn't move a muscle for this whole two hours or so, while the rest of us were being still for a while and then going to look out the window and check.
I don't know, maybe there weren't cell phones yet.
I think there weren't, so we couldn't even do that.
We're just like, he's going to come.
He's going to make it somehow.
And then I found out later from them that that was total SOP for Trampa Rinpoche.
He would often show up a couple of hours late for lectures.
It was expected.
So they were just in their element.
So anyway, it's funny how powerful these memories are when you're in a new Zen retreat.
Ten years, twenty years, thirty years later, you remember these things.
Maybe we're creating a powerful memory that you'll use in a talk one day, twenty years from now.
You never know.
But anyway, waiting is good for us.
We're not good at it.
We need practice at waiting.
That's what we're doing anyway: nothing but waiting.
But we get a little frustrated too, because what are we waiting for?
We don't know.
What am I waiting for?
Waiting for something.
So I really appreciated Alison's talk yesterday.
It's so wonderful to have new expressions of the Dharma just pop up.
Like that guy coming to give the talk way back when.
What a great case to bring out.
Because we seem like we're waiting for stuff, right?
We're waiting for the right insight or the right state of mind.
The right feeling.
Finally.
And definitely we like to have the right things, whether we admit it or not.
We're all sort of gear junkies.
Pretty nicely outfitted here, huh?
We get compliments.
Yes, you hear that?
She made a compliment.
Beautiful Zen-do.
Yes.
We have the right things.
It's recognizably a Zen-do.
But maybe that case is really right.
We should probably pay a lot more attention and be a lot more interested in waiting for no mind.
Waiting for no Buddha.
Waiting for no thing.
And a little scholarly sidebar, in case you're interested in these things.
Another reason these koan stories are so hard to keep track of and make sense of is that there are so many different ways the teachers' names are given.
The names are actually pairs of Chinese characters.
Same character.
But we're doing this in English, so we can't see the character.
Alison was reading a Japanese commentary on the Mumonkan.
It talked about the teacher Nansen, who is the same as the teacher Nanshuan.
And Nansen is the teacher of Joshu, which is the same as saying Nanshuan is the teacher of Jiaojiao.
So, are you confused yet?
Even the Chinese have more than one way to pronounce these characters.
And then the Japanese.
It's just so fascinating.
Like most of East Asia, Chinese culture and literature is the high culture, and so the Japanese imported that as best they could.
But they must not have had any Chinese people hanging around at the time, because then they made up their own ways of saying all the different Chinese characters.
So instead of Kuan, Sen; instead of Jiao, Zhou.
And I guess we're just doing the same thing, because however I'm trying to say the Chinese is surely wrong anyway.
If there were an actual Chinese person, they'd be like, what?
What was that?
So anyway, that's who she was speaking about, characters we've heard of before.
Jiaojiao, Nanshuan.
But back to finding the mind.
Waiting for the mind.
Waiting for the no mind.
I thought Dogen had some good advice for us this morning, didn't you think?
He had a lot of advice for us.
It went by pretty fast.
But I was noticing particularly this part this morning.
*When you find your place where you are, practice occurs, actualizing the fundamental point.
When you find your way at this moment, practice occurs, actualizing the fundamental point.
For the place, the way, is neither large nor small, neither yours nor others.
The place, the way, has not carried over from the past.
It's not merely arising now.
Accordingly, in the practice, enlightenment of the Buddha way, to attain one thing is to penetrate one thing.
To meet one practice is to sustain one practice.*
Typical Dogen conclusion, right?
How do you get there?
But this idea of finding your place where you are has a feeling to it, doesn't it?
That sounds good.
We would all like to find our place where we are, I think.
And it sounds like a thing to do.
That there must have been a time before you did the practices when you didn't find your place where you were or where you are, and then maybe one day you'll find it.
And let that be great.
It does have the word "when" in there, at least in our translation: when you find your place where you are.
Sounds like there's going to be a before and an after.
Although not too many paragraphs before, he was totally refuting the idea that before and after make any sense, too.
Did you notice that?
About firewood and seasons and stuff.
Before and after doesn't make any sense.
But when you find your place where you are, then.
So this made me think of a few lines of Wendell Berry that someone was just reminding me of.
*It may be that when you no longer know what to do, we have come to our real work.
It may be when we no longer know what to do, we have come to our real work.
And that when we no longer know which way to go, we have come to our real journey.
The mind that is not baffled is not employed.
The impeded stream is the one that sings.*
This is good for us in sesshin.
*It may be when we no longer know what to do, we have come to our real work.
And when we no longer know which way to go, we have come to our real journey.
The mind that is not baffled is not employed.
The impeded stream is the one that sings.*
How do these poets do that?
The impeded stream is the one that sings.
So maybe that's like finding the not place or the no place, right where we are or right where we aren't.
Maybe it's when we realize that we can't find it.
We've all had this experience, I think, when we finally let go and give up and realize this is getting me nowhere.
I'm just spinning my wheels here.
And it's painful in the body, right?
You're like, I've got to figure this out.
We're so very good at tension injection.
I'm going to inject more tension, that will help.
And you can do that for a while and it may look like you've got the thing here.
Like, I bet I look pretty good now in my posture.
But actually you're just getting tense.
Trying hard when you really are completely baffled.
So how's it going in your zazen practice in sesshin here?
Are you trying, trying, trying to find your place where you are and not finding it?
Or are you finding it?
Or maybe you have to try hard for a while until you get so tired of trying that you let go of trying.
Maybe that's how it needs to go.
Maybe you need to inject a lot of tension before you give it up.
But Dogen goes on to talk about the qualities of this place.
He said:
*The place, the way,*
so it's a place or a way,
*is neither large nor small, neither yours nor others.
The place, the way, has not carried over from the past, and it's not merely arising now.*
It's not large nor small.
It's not a big deal.
It's not a small deal.
Neither yours nor others: it's not something you can even make happen.
And it's not something you can get from somebody else, if you just had the right advice or the right teacher or something, the right books.
It hasn't carried over from the past, and it's not merely arising now.
So it's not something we receive, like we always say, this ancient way we receive from our ancestors.
He says, no, no, no.
Too small.
Too big.
Not that.
And he even refutes the whole idea of the present moment in there too.
It's not merely arising now.
That would really cheapen it if it was just something that was arising now.
So it's somehow beyond size and location and ownership and making it happen, not making it happen, and it's beyond time.
But the good news is that it is enough.
Which is to say that we are enough.
*To attain one thing is to penetrate one thing,* he says.
*To meet one practice is to sustain one practice.*
So it's complete.
All we have to do is find our place where we are, actualizing the fundamental point.
That's all we have to do.
So actualizing the fundamental point, by the way, is a translation of the title of the essay, Genjokoan.
And you can read many long essays about the meaning of those two words, four characters, but more or less it's the koan, the engagement of our life.
We could say everyday life, as if there were not an everyday life, but just our life, our experience, our existence.
The koan of our existence.
Find your place where you are and then you're in that.
You're with it.
You're fully there.
You're coursing in the koan of life.
Does that mean you've got something figured out?
I'm going to have to read much Dogen to know the answer to that.
Or Wendell Berry.

It may be easier for us, poor sods, that it may be when we no longer know what to do, that we've come to our real work, and we no longer know which way to go, we've come to our real journey, and can we actually embrace that?
Even if we don't understand it in that way that we so want to understand things.
And Dogen goes on a little later in the essay that we chanted this morning.
Right after that he says:
*Do not suppose that what you attain becomes your knowledge and is grasped by your intellect.
Although actualized immediately, what is inconceivable may not be apparent.
Its emergence is beyond your knowledge.*
Something that cheers us up a little bit, if we feel frustrated or something.
Maybe we already found our place where we are.
We just don't know it.
It's not graspable in that kind of knowing way.
It's inconceivable.
It's beyond our knowledge.
So what do we do with all this?
What is it we're doing here?
If we can't grasp it, how do we operate?
How do we orient?
How do we do or non-do whatever it is that we're trying to do or non-do?
Of course the mind wants to make language about all this, and here I am talking on and on using language.
So what are the right words?
What are the skillful words?
To point ourselves towards this Actualizing the fundamental point, to encourage ourselves to realize or find or feel or discover or remember that we can find our place right where we are.
What are the right words?
What are the wrong words?
Is it about words?
Maybe it's not about words at all.
Maybe it's about silence.
We've been also doing our best here, I think.
Pretty quiet, mostly, around the place.
To express the truth with silence.
To express the Dharma with silence.
To express ourselves with silence.
You practice silence for a while, you realize that words seem so crude, right?
So approximate, coarse.
Even the most refined words.
Doesn't silence have a different feeling to it?
That kind of expression, silence, expression.
So, words and silence are what case 24 of the Mumonkan seems to be about.
This is the case that I once unconsciously skipped in my little project here.
And then yesterday, or day four yesterday, I consciously skipped it and I got a little schooling from Alison about it.
So I think it's time for case 24.
You ready?
Are you ready?
I wasn't ready before, but maybe now I'm ready.
What does it mean to be ready anyway?
So here's the case.
*A monk asked Fenghsueh, "Both speech and silence include separation and union.
How can we escape these faults?"*
So the question of the teacher here is, speech and silence include separation and union.
How can we escape these faults?
Fenghsueh, the teacher, replied:
*"I always remember spring in Xiang Nan, where the partridges sing, how fragrant the countless flowers."*
You can imagine a big grin on his face.
I remember the spring in Xiang Nan where the partridges sing, how fragrant the countless flowers.
I remember late July in Heather Meadows, the gray jays flit by and the heather flowers.
So, speech and silence.
Speech does separate.
Separation and union.
Speech separates, which we need to do, I think.
This is helpful.
We have to be able to distinguish things and separate them and understand them from different angles.
And how can we do that if we don't peel things apart with our concepts and our words and our ideas?
That's how we learn about the world, right?
We're like a little child who takes things apart.
Rips the toy apart to understand how it works.
It's like the young Dalai Lama.
There were some Western toys lying around that explorers and visitors had left behind, although Tibet was mostly isolated from the West, even in his early lifetime.
So he'd take them apart, and usually be able to put them back together, but not always.
So we need concepts so we can take things apart.
But it's also a huge problem for us, as we know, because then we are believing in our illusion that things are separate.
We extrapolate way beyond taking apart a toy car to taking apart each other, taking apart our world.
Then we have all kinds of violence and wars and political strife and the whole deal.
Interpersonal problems.
Like what really goes on at the Zen Center, you know?
So we need speech, but it's a problem.
And we need silence, too, because silence supports union, right?
Silence supports everything being together.
Seamless, right?
A seamless whole.
So beautiful.
Somebody was telling me, "I don't know why we do this all day, but there's these moments, you know?
The bell rings and you just hear it ringing through the silence and the overtones of it."
But it's the silence that allows the bell to ring, right?
The refuges at the end, when we managed to harmonize.
Last night, not so much, but usually.
So beautiful, emerging from the silence, you know?
And even without anything emerging in it, we start to gradually notice, even without needing that contrast of an emerging sound, we start to hear and feel and taste and touch silence.
So peaceful.
So beautiful, you know?
Fragile, too, right?
It just takes one person kind of grousing out loud.
The silence gets blown to pieces and we have to all run around and try to get it back.
So it's beautiful.
It's extra beautiful because it's fragile.
But there's also something a little deceptive, right?
A little easy to misunderstand about silence.
We could get a little fuzzy, a little vague, a little hazy.
It's so peaceful and silent in here, you know?
None of you are talking, and I'm going to choose to assume you are peaceful and happy and glad to be here, glad to be with your colleagues, you know?
Beautiful.
And I know that's not really true.
Kind of is.
Kind of not, you know?
Who knows what's going on in the silence?
And of course, in bigger ways, this side of reality is easy to kind of smother the world with, you know?

So these two words that are being referred to here in English as separation and union, the results of speech and silence, turned out to be a reference to a fifth century Chinese Buddhist text, and the commentary to this case tries to explain that.
It just drives me nuts.
You know, what do I know about Chinese philosophy?
That's part of what bunged me up.
And then I started comparing different translations, and they were all so different.
So the one I read you:
*Both speech and silence include separation and union.
How can we escape these faults?*
Here's another one:
*Speech and silence involve alienation and vagueness.
How does one go through without transgression?*
Similar.
Here's another one where he adds all kinds of words to try to explain the whole thing.
Sorry, let me start over.
This one's hard.
*Speech becomes less and less until it reaches the limit, which is called ri, yet is unable to express reality.
Silence becomes deeper and deeper until it reaches the limit, which is called bi, yet it is not able to express reality.
There must be a way to express reality beyond both ri and bi.
Please show me the way.*
So whether or not we're ever going to understand what they mean here by these characters, ri and bi, this idea of reaching the limit is interesting, though.
Speech becomes less and less until it reaches the limit, yet is unable to express reality.
Silence becomes deeper and deeper until it reaches the limit, and yet is unable to express reality.
One last one.
Here's Robert Aitken.
Stand by around here.
*Speech and silence are concerned with equality and differentiation.
How can I transcend equality and differentiation?*
Maybe he was thinking of our chant, the emerging of difference in unity, san do kai.
He picked those words.
So we are all now properly tangled up, like the monk was, like I was, so I was intimidated to give a talk about this darn case.
And how does the teacher answer?
Well, he could have chosen silence, and there are many examples of this in the literature of Zen.
He could have refused to answer, which would have been a pretty good answer, right?
One day, one of us will have the chutzpah to do a proper Zen talk, where we get up here and just don't say a word for half an hour.
And be sure and press the recorder, too, so that we record the silence.
That's advanced teaching.
We're not ready yet.
So that would have been a good answer, you know?
Or, he's probably a pretty smart teacher.
He could have explained this Chinese philosophy probably pretty well.
Instead, he says, "Ah, I always remember the spring in Qiongnan, where the partridges sing, and how fragrant the countless flowers."
And it's funny, that has like a familiar feeling to it, even though we have no idea where Qiongnan is.
Maybe we've not been anywhere where partridges are in the trees, you know?
We've probably noticed blooming flowers before.
So the particulars are lost to us, but there's a feeling to this expression, isn't there?
The flowers are blooming.
The moon is out.
The morning star rises in the east.
That's the answer.
That's the answer to our tangle between silence and speech.
Which makes us think, I think, a little bit of what I quoted from Suzuki Roshi, whenever that was.

Remember, he's going on about the hundred foot pole, and how it was a mistake to think that you were at the top, because there is no top, and you can't sit, and you can't jump, and therefore what do you do?
You sit, and you jump, naturally.
And then he ends that part by saying, you forget all about yourself, and you are refreshed.
You are a new self, and before that self becomes an old self, you say yes, and walk to the kitchen for breakfast.
Walk to the kitchen for breakfast.
You go on a walk in our little tiny garden in back, admire the ferns.
You look up at the sky.
You actually take a minute to really notice what it feels like to breathe.
Why was I so tangled up?
I can't remember.
Because when you no longer know what to do, your real work has begun.
You no longer know where to go.
And so where do you go?
Here.
Right here.
So I want to meet Alison's roomie and collar one.
This is not a competition.
Don't worry.
So here's a little piece by Rumi called Bird Wings that makes me think of all this.
*Your grief for what you've lost lifts a mirror up to where you're bravely working.
Expecting the worst, you look.
And instead, here's the joyful face you've been waiting to see.
Your hand opens and closes and opens and closes.
If it were always a fist, or always stretched open, you'd be paralyzed.
Your presence is in every small, contracting and expanding.
The two as beautifully balanced and coordinated as bird wings.*
Your grief.
Don't miss that word.
*Your grief for what you've lost lifts a mirror up to where you're bravely working.
Expecting the worst, you look.
And instead, here's the joyful face you've been waiting to see.
Your hand opens and closes and opens and closes.
If it were always a fist, or always stretched open, you'd be paralyzed.
Your deepest presence in every small, contracting and expanding.
The two as beautifully balanced and coordinated as bird wings.*
You have to have both wings.
So it's good not to forget that there's a lot of grief in this practice, in this work, that we don't know what words and silence to use exactly for.
It's good not to be fooled by all the Zen calm that's apparently hanging around here.
Not to fool yourself, mostly.
And we are kind of calm, right?
It is good to be a little more calm, the more possible for us to operate, you know?
But it's not really about the calm.
We're also grieving.
Each of us lost so much.
And it's hard to face the losses.
And yet, when we finally muster the courage to face our losses, expecting the worst.
Really expecting the worst, right?
Don't you think you expect the worst?
Somehow we see joy is woven in there, too.
With the sadness, with the pain, with the loss.
And that there's no way forward but through.
You can't avoid this.
You can't use your practice to avoid this.
You can try.
And maybe in our exploration we need both of these, right?
We need the open hand of silence.
We could all use a lot more silence, I bet.
And the closed fist of words and concepts and plans and psychology and all the stuff.
Philosophy, teachings, science.
But I like this image.
They need to be balanced.
Or even the balance of them.
But your deepest presence is in every small contraction and expansion.
And it seems we do need to divide things up the way we do.
But maybe through practice we can remember that it's not really divided up that way.
That we need our thinking and we need our non-thinking, and we don't have to try so damn hard to figure out Dogen's no-thinking, non-thinking, blah, blah, blah.
Maybe we just show up for our life as it is.
With our suffering, with our confusion, with our losses.
With our joy, you know.
With our confidence.
With our incredible resilience.
Maybe what we need is some kind of union of silence and speech.
And it's okay if there's too much B or too little B or whatever the hell those are, you know.
Maybe we can trust the system to take care of that without our needing to figure out or intervene too much.
Just letting the hand open and close.
Letting the words arise and go back to silence.
Not holding on to the silence either.
But we could probably, all of us, use a few thousand days of sesshin nonetheless, you know.
To sit in silence.
You good for us?
But not because the silence has the answers.
Because contracting and expanding, the two as beautifully balanced and coordinated as bird wings, because the impeded stream is the one that sings.
And that, according to all this, is good: to be baffled.
So hopefully I've successfully baffled you.
I baffled myself pretty good.
Let's continue our sesshin.
Thanks everybody.
What a blessing to get to do this together, huh?
Even when we don't feel like it's a blessing, it's especially a blessing then.
